title: The Master Mega Game Graphics and Style Discussion Thread

posts.author: Ms Littlefish
posts.body:
Yes…this is the new home of the monthly RTP debate thread. Not to exhaust everyone after this month’s issue, but perhaps some sort of multi-purpose pinned discussion is long overdue? My finger can forever be placed on “merge post.”
OH! But, let’s make it so much more than RTP babble!
Let’s use this place to discuss any number of topics surrounding game graphics. Since we’re over here in general discussion, it should be geared toward graphics for RPG Maker games though it’s natural other games will need discussed to make thorough analysis.
Ideas of discussions!
What makes a graphic style age well?
How do you decide what direction to take your graphics?
What styles do you prefer?
How do your graphics elevate and become part of the narrative?
Sky’s the limit. Just remember to direct your very
specific
“how do I graphic?” questions to the Resource Support sections.

posts.author: Timeline_man
posts.body: I'm probably in the minority of gamers, but I like styles of graphics that are unique and stand out, even if they're "ugly". I also find that these types of styles age better, since they tend to look a specific way, and the advancement of technology rarely plays into how that style can be achieved, but that's far from a universal statement.

posts.author: Iron_Brew
posts.body:
Before I get into it, apologies in advance for the length of this post. I know brevity is the soul of wit and all that, but I think there's an element of this discussion that always gets overlooked, so I figured I'd write down my thoughts on what that thing is, and how we can be healthier in our discussion of the RTP (and other asset packs) in general!
So, here's the issue as I see it with the RTP, and I think it's the secret sauce of why so many RM games - and games by solodevs in general - end up looking visually messy, or unappealing:
Art Direction
​
Above and beyond the skill of creating individual assets for a video game, be they characters, environments, props, or "other", there is a skill which unifies how all of those assets look
for that project.
This is what we call 'Art Direction', and it is probably more important to the way the audience feel about your game's visuals than any individual piece of art within the game.
Think of any game that "looks good" and you'll generally be able to identify the deliberate decisions (or direction) given, or taken, to end up with the visual qualities the game eventually extolls. It can be the difference between a generic shooter and - for example - Borderlands, or Call of Duty. Art Direction isn't as simple as "style", and depending on the scope and fidelity of the project can also encompass things like lighting, UI/UX work, and everything the game does visually to make the player think, feel, or act a certain way.
Another thing games that "look good" tend to also have is artistic cohesion. They tend not to be eclectic mismatches of assets, hamfistedly edited in Gimp to try to fit into an existing style - everything is done with purpose (again, read as Direction) to ensure that the end product that the player sees is
appealing
and
tonally appropriate
to the game being played.
As an analogy, try to think of the difference between Art and Art Direction as a painting in a gallery, with each member of the team (or, in solo projects, each function) at different levels of distance from an individual painting:
Artists ensure that each individual brushstroke is properly placed and works with the strokes around it. They are as close to the canvas as possible to ensure that this is the case.
More senior artists, or Leads, ensure that those individual brushstrokes make up whatever the subject being painted is - be it a person, an object, or a scene. They stand far enough away from the canvas to ensure they can see the bit of the painting for which they (and their artists) are responsible for.
The Art Director makes sure that the painting itself looks good. He stands as far from the painting as other viewers and makes calls that change the style of the painting, how everything is composed, and in general what
direction
the painting takes.
Now, how does this apply to the RTP?
​
The thing to remember about the RTP - and any stock assets that aren't handcrafted for a project - is that they are, by definition, generic. I don't mean "generic" in any negative way here, but rather in its most literal definition:
They are generic because they have to be used in a wide variety of projects, and as such are direction-agnostic.
This is where the weakness of any generic/stock assets come in - and it's why (I think) so many RTP games can come across as visually underwhelming. The assets themselves have been created by really talented artists close to the canvas, and the leads overseeing them know what they are and have ensured quality in that way. The issue is that the direction here is that these have to fit with a broad variety of tones, so that they can fit into
as many projects as possible
.
Does that mean that the RTP is bad?
​
Absolutely not.
It is cohesive, competently made, and for projects that fit that generic fantasy style they can absolutely be appropriate. There's also a ton you can do to the RTP to alter the tone of the art drastically.
What I do think is that because of the issue of generic Art Direction the assets in the RTP - and the RTP as a whole - will be
sub optimal
for projects which rely heavily on art to set any tone the RTP was not designed for. If supplemented poorly by assets not created in the style of the RTP you also end up with issues around artistic cohesion; great games, but when players look at them their reaction isn't "this looks great", it's "why do the characters not fit with the world?"
This means that the RTP also then becomes quite constricting in terms of which assets you are able to use (if you want to create a game which is visually cohesive).
There are absolutely a ton of great games that can be made using just the RTP - and with limited tilesets in general (see
Link's Awakening
for a great example of this), but I don't think that's really what we should be concerning ourselves with. The argument has been made for and against the RTP so many times that I think a lot of people are blue in the face, and sick of people going back and forth on it: I think that this is because we're focused on "is it ok to use this", or "is it good/bad", rather than "what are the pros and cons of using the RTP".
If you re-frame the discussion around that I think that a lot of the qualitative concerns people have surrounding the argument somewhat fall away. The RTP is great because it's free, cohesive, and relatively comprehensive. It's less great because it's generic, precludes the use of custom assets in different styles, and has associations in the public eye (on the
rare
occasion that people do identify it as 'those RPG maker assets') with shovelware and pornography.
In general, as with all things, I think it's best to be deliberate about what it is you're making.
If you have the time, aptitude, or budget then there is absolutely a benefit to having a game made with custom, art-directed assets that help you convey tone (and don't betray your tone or narrative because you're forced into decisions by usiing the RTP).
If you don't, then just use the RTP - but don't get salty when people say "the art here doesn't really line up with what you're trying to do". The flat facts of it are that it simply won't (to the same extent as custom, directed art would), because if you try to pretzel art with different direction, style, or technical specs into something they're
not meant to be used for
you will end up with compromises that affect the way your game is seen.
That doesn't mean the RTP is bad, or that it shouldn't be used, or that it's even sub-optimal for some applications, but I think it's healthier to talk about what it's good at rather than endlessly arguing about the viability of a set of generic assets included for free with RPG Maker.
After all, most people don't know what the RTP even is, and as I always say: The audience for your game is not other devs, it's players!
Thanks for your time!

Thank you for typing this out. This actually really helps out on a question I made in another forum area, as you actually found my post haha.
Reframing it as pros and cons cleared things up in my brain just like that. For me, there are more pros than cons to using certain parts of the RTP.
As a separate thought:
I feel like, for me, it's based on time and energy versus what is appealing to the widest audience. And, I really like the style of the battle sprites and tilesets! They are objectively good, depending on the project. There's also a lot of room for creativity using them!
The RTP assets open the door to allow a lot of creators in who wouldn't be able to otherwise. I consider that to be a good thing, while some consider it to be 'bad'! I'd rather have a million 'bad' games and allow people to be creative in ways they want to be!

posts.author: Kenen
posts.body:
I personally love MV's RTP, but it doesn't align with the characters that I have in mind, and the restrictive nature that
@Iron_Brew
points out is definitely a limiting factor. But it doesn't stop me from frequently thinking about putting together some sort of small adventure with H, T, M, and L!
That aside, I think it's important to do one of two things: lean in to your personal skillset, or lean in to what you want to learn—because RPG Maker presents great learning opportunities.
Maybe you have a really endearing art style like Iron Brew or any of the other talented artists here on the forums. So, maybe you capitalize on that and work toward crafting your own RTP, or enhancing the RTP with custom assets.
Or, maybe you have experience with UI design, so you focus on presenting the RTP in new ways that vary from the established plugin libraries that everyone has seen over and over again.
Consider your skills, and consider what you want to learn from the process. If your skillset or learning objectives don't consist of replacing the RTP, then consider choosing the RTP or asset pack(s) that best align with those skills or goals.
The idea is to enhance the ready-made assets with the skills that you personally bring to the table.
As a side-note, I personally wouldn't put much emphasis on the concept of what is going to appeal to an audience. Practice scope control. If your project is purely for personal enrichment or something to share with your friends, does it really matter if X number of people on Reddit or Steam hate the RTP?
Probably not.

posts.author: Candacis
posts.body:
I think the MV rtp is great and if you use it with the Trinity dlc even more so. Avery made a great tutorial showcasing how to adjust it to fit the FSM dlc.
The Mz rtp has its good and weak parts (the autotiles are its weak parts).
But both are free, if you own the maker and matching custom tiles also available here in the forum.
And making a custom tileset could take as long as making a game in itself. It is mainly a question on what you enjoy more. Making a game or making assets for it.

posts.author: Milennin
posts.body:
Big fan of the RTP. But I'm more of a gameplay and mechanics guy, and I'd rather play a well thought out game using RTP than a shallow game using all custom graphics. When I look for a random RPG Maker game to play, I'll usually seek out something that involves RTP because I enjoy seeing what people can do with limited resources. And the RTP oozes that RPG Maker charm that you can't find anywhere else.
The only time I'd avoid RTP as the plague is when I'm looking to spend money on a game. I associate the RTP with free hobby projects, and I'm not willing to spend a dime on a game that makes use of it.

posts.author: Ms Littlefish
posts.body:
I really think
@Iron_Brew
…that you cover so many of my feelings. There are more cons for me (I have a pretty specific atmosphere and world building I want the direction of my art to facilitate…but the RTP is neither good nor bad. It is not a living being with morals. The reasons
why
people want to make a game are way too vast to prescribe a single roadmap.
What I
will
say is that any premade graphic is a tool and the most critical issue is how people use their tools. There are many topics people can study and get a better understanding of without even needing to place a pen to a paper…or err, tablet. I talk about it ad nauseam, really…but color theory and composition.
Having even a baseline understanding of how colors pair and mix, how to create harmonies and schemes…what makes a composition and how to control positive and negative space (and choosing where to run off the canvas and where not to) can take a map (no matter the graphics you’re using) from “not visually offensive” to “I can’t stop looking at it.” To me,
these
are core art skills and it’s
why
there are art modes that are focused solely on color, shape, and composition.
Simple recolors and purposefully placing all the objects on your maps are significantly more powerful than I think people realize. And…that all can happen despite whatever tile you use.
I really, really, REALLY love Yoshi’s Island and its use of color is to die for. I could gush about this game’s graphics for quite a while.  The background uses primarily tertiary colors. Looking at the color wheel, you will even notice that the sky and the grasses/bushes offset each other on the wheel. And even further, the orange flowers are still leaning into  the tertiary. So…we are working with a pretty classic color harmony here and it #justworksTM
Even further, the foreground objects become a LOT more primary and it really helps bring them “closer” to the player despite being on the 2D space without even using any aggressive shading styles.

posts.author: BubblegumPatty
posts.body:
I really like the RTP! My only real gripes with it is it's a bit slim on options without relying on free resources or DLC (and potentially editing those resources/DLC). But eh, that's life.  What's there is solid.
In general, I will say I'm not the pickiest with graphics. If the story and/or gameplay is good enough, I'll tolerate the ugliest or worst aged graphics known to man. My only bar is that I know what I'm looking at most of the time, and I would
really like it
if what's I'm seeing was all the same style. One game i've played bugged me with how it uses a bunch of different styles all over, and I refuse to use any mods/CC in the sims or skyrim where the models are too highly rendered because it clashes with the rest of the game.
As far as aging, stylized always ages the best, especially in 3d. I have my gripes with the sims 4, but a decade out it still looks pretty good with it's cartoony graphics while the sims 3 looks.... very potato-y. At best.

Not entirely related to the core topic of the thread, but for those less artistically inclined, especially when it comes to the visual stuff, this tool is a great starting point for picking colors:
Paletton - The Color Scheme Designer
In love with colors, since 2002. A designer tool for creating color combinations that work together well. Formerly known as Color Scheme Designer. Use the color wheel to create great color palettes.
paletton.com
I use this thing A Ton to at least get me a base-line with my colors. When I was in University my teacher provided this resource to me. Somehow this website still exists and still functions just as well.
Obviously how and where you use the colors is up to you (which may require some artistic determination) but at least you got the baseline covered.

posts.author: Ms Littlefish
Willibab
posts.body:
I don't think the RTP is bad, just overused. And I personally get tired of seeing the same thing over and over regardless of the quality of other features.
And if you're thinking ''ofc its overused, it comes with the engine and not everyone can make their own''  Yes, true. But there being reasons for something being the way it is doesn't change the fact that it still is.
I also just straight up dislike Chibi stuff so that doesnt help.

posts.author: TMS
posts.body:
As someone who can’t create graphics, or music, or code (apart from very simple edits of existing code), I pretty much have to rely either on the RTP or material I can buy or download from elsewhere, so it’s always been a little discouraging how many people won’t consider playing games with RTP graphics. Of course, I can also understand, given the circumstances, why people would be wary of the RTP. Ideally, every game would use material unique to itself, but that requires a lot of time, effort, and (in most cases) money. I have a number of ideas for what might be called “dream games,” and would certainly prefer that they use graphics (and other material) created specially for them. My current plan, as I’ve mentioned elsewhere, is to turn these “game” ideas into novels (since writing is the one art form I’m good at), which can then hopefully be used to draw in collaborators.
In the meantime, my desire to create games (using RPG Maker, which is about the only game development software simple enough for me to use) remains, and I think I may mess around with the RTP when the urge hits to maybe make this happen. I don’t know yet to what extent I will, on the one hand, try to adapt my interests to the RTP and, on the other hand, allow the RTP to inspire me. I’m sure the project will do both of these things to some degree, but probably the latter would be best. If anyone has any thoughts on the issue, I’d love to hear them.
Since I noticed someone alluded to it above, and I’ve been wondering about it for a while, is there a similar stigma hanging about the “DLC” products that there is about the RTP? Is it perhaps less, because RM users don’t have access to the DLC by default?
Edit:
I forgot to mention that at times the RTP doesn’t do a great job of unified art direction. The battle backgrounds are out of scale with the enemy battlers, so that Treants look less like tree-giants and more like tree-munchkins. And of course the side-view actor battlers in the newer platforms are ridiculously tiny in comparison to both the backgrounds and the enemies. This is something that is one of the RTP’s biggest faults, in my opinion.

posts.author: TRIDIUM

posts.author: TeiRaven
posts.body:
To paraphrase what I've said before about this: think of the RTP like the box of eight crayola crayons. It will get you started, and some people can do really amazing things with just that and nothing else. Most people will want to get more colors of crayons later. Some people will switch to markers. Some people end up preferring modeling clay. All of those things are perfectly okay!
The RTP will get you started, and some people can do really amazing things with just that and nothing else. Most people will want to get more RTP-style assets later. Some people will switch to other pixel-art-style graphics, like Time Fantasy. Some people end up making their own assets from scratch. All of those things are perfectly okay!
For a hobbyist, the most important thing is that you're having fun. When you're making games to pay the bills,
then
you can worry about what will sell--but for now, focus on enjoying yourself and learning the engine.

Upon reading the previous page and more relevant to the thread on the whole--
@NaMosca
, if you're making a non-commercial project just for fun, for your own enjoyment and nothing else, then you should do what you want. If you
want
to use exclusively RTP and the existing systems, then that's what you should do.
But
, if you're looking to appeal to a wider audience, I agree with Martin and Slaughty both. XP is far and away my favorite RTP, and--because it's older--it's somewhat less common than the other RTPs. Both of the games to my name use the XP RTP style, and both have gotten a lot of compliments on the art. I know my other XP-using friends get the same sort of comments. It's a surprisingly popular look!
However, I think you're doing yourself a disservice if you
only
use the RTP. XP has a great variety of tilesets and characters, for example, but the icons are a little lackluster. If your game is centered heavily on crafting, as you say, then I would strongly recommend looking for addtional resources that go with that theme! Avery has some great tiles of things like looms and forges, and her icons are
incredible.
Adding custom icons would be huge, for giving your game that extra bit of polish. Especially for differentiating crafting materials in your inventory! There are lots of simple, little ways like that to make your game stand out.
The thing I would specifically caution against would be using the default characters in a game without a lot of dialogue. There's an argument to be made for the fun of making a game using the RTP to see how much you can build upon it (why is Aluxes so determined to be a hero? Where did Gloria learn to heal? etc etc etc) but if you're not planning to do something story-heavy, I think you'd be shooting yourself in the foot to use the characters that come with the program as part of your core cast--especially if they're mixed in with characters of your own creation.
Just my two cents!

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
This is just the opinion of an old zombie who is often the outlier in perspectives. I'm also still new to RPG Maker developing (3 years) and I'm not really fond of the RTP graphics in general. I'm not generally a chibi fan or a fan of JRPGs.
With all that said, for people who are just developing games as a hobby, I'd say just use the RTP until you actually have a decent game put together. Then, if you want to invest time transitioning from the RTP to other options, then cool.
If you enjoy making your own assets or are interested in learning and want to put in the work, then I'd say go in that direction.
If you have a decent game put together and you are willing and able to invest money on paid assets, then that's cool too.
If you want to make a commercial game where you want a chance to make any amount of money, then I'd say you need to treat it as a business investment and use something other than the RTP.
I'm also an outlier because I don't look at graphics and sound first in a game. I primarily focus on game play and mechanics. So personally, I'd give a game with RTP assets a chance if it looked like a game that I would enjoy.
My Sudoku game doesn't use much RTP, but I did make the decision to include ALL the music from ALL the RPG Makers. As a nod to the engine that is making my game possible. And I also included a lot of free music as well.
Most of the games I want to make won't use the RTP tile sets, sprites, etc.
And just as an aside, when it comes to reading Steam reviews for games I'm interested in, I completely ignore the ones that complain about the RTP being used. I find using the default RM combat mechanics more offensive than using the RTP assets. But that's just me.
As a last point, I don't think using the RTP has any bearing on making a decent game. You can make an incredible game using just stick figures. At least from my perspective. But making a marketable game? I think using the RTP would make that much more difficult.
Good luck on your projects!

posts.author: Solar_Flare
posts.body:
I do use default assets. I will probably always use default assets in every RPGMaker game that I make, but the degree may vary.
The current game I'm working on uses
mostly
default assets (MV). The general trend is that if there's a default asset for something I need, then I use it. I only look for non-default assets when the default ones are missing what I need.
I have another game in early stages that'll probably work out the same (but for MZ).
On the other hand, I also have another game planned where I intend to replace nearly all the default assets with custom assets. However, there will still be
some
default assets. The entire default SE library will still be included, and likely the BGS and ME as well (but not the BGM). I'm still undecided on how much of the default tilesets to use. Probably all the default animation frames will be used as well. Other things I
may
use from the RTP include the default SV weapons, SV state overlays, and balloon icons; some of the battlebacks and parallaxes; and the object characters (character sheets whose name begins with
!
).
The one part of the RTP that I would never discard is the SE library.
In general, I would never recommend that someone completely ignore the RTP. At the very least, use the SE library. And if you happen to like the chibi style, there's no real reason to shun the RTP characters. If one of them happens to be a perfect (or near-perfect) fit for your character, use it (maybe with a few edits).
The one thing I would generally recommend no-one use from the RTP (except for very casual games, or maybe contests where there's a tight time limit) is the titlescreen images. I think every game should really have its own unique titlescreen image (maybe even more than one, if that suits your game). Although, to be clear, that only means I don't think they should be used
as the titlescreen
. Some of them would make decent battlebacks, so using them in that way would be fine.

I have used 3 methods for having smaller sprites in the overworld:
1) Running common events whenever the party enters or leaves the overworld to change the sprites for all actors that might be in the party. [The smaller sprites can be made with GIMP.]
2) Plugin by Aramis called "SpriteZoom". You can resize sprites including the player character and followers during the game. You still need to run common events whenever the party enters or leaves the overworld, but you don't need to muck-about with graphics yourself. This is a very flexible plugin; you can have some characters on the same map small, others normal size, and others larger than normal.
3) Plugin by Shio_inu called "PD_AdjustCharaSprite". All sprites including the party, followers and events are automatically shrunk on the overworld unless they are taken from the tile sheets or the name of the sprite-sheet includes 'noAdjust'. No need for common events to alter sprite size! As written, there seems to be a bug that affects it if the sprite filename includes a capital 'F'. This is my current choice.
Edit
: Half-sized sprites for the party and any NPC seems about right for both the default overworld tiles and the Winlu ones. I understand that the results from either using GIMP or the plugin shrinking the sprites in game tend to be better making them 50% than other ratios.

posts.author: LaCipolla
posts.body:
Perhaps a hot take, but this stigma is practically only relevant for players who dabbled in the rpg maker scene at one point in their life, and even then, what qualifies as "standard" varies wildly. (For me, RM2k assets are far more recognizable than the modern stuff. I couldn't even tell you what VX looked like. ^^) Outside of the scene, 99% of players would't recognize any standard assets – IF they know what an "rpg maker" is in the first place.
My first quasi-commercial game was made was with RMMZ assets only, and practically no one in the Steam reviews complained about it. Even the general "2D snes look" came up more often, usually as an issue of personal taste.
Still, the stigma in the scene is already a factor when going in a more professional direction. In my recent game, I'm only using some of these assets very intentionally (e.g. for the main character).
Either way, people underestimate how good and versatile these assets have been, in every version and especially for beginners! I would stand by them any day.
That goes double when it comes to less "obvious" stuff like music, sounds and special effects, btw! The RMMZ music is extremely nice and adaptable. I am only getting somewhat tired of it after two whole games.
